draft.title: United States involvement
card: The United States feared that if one country in Southeast Asia became communist, its neighbours would follow, like falling dominoes. This idea is called the domino theory.
At first the US gave money and weapons and sent military advisers to train South Vietnam's army. Advisers were not sent to fight.

In August 1964, US ships reported attacks by North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin. Congress then passed a resolution that let President Johnson use military force in Vietnam without a declaration of war.
In 1965 the first US combat troops landed. Australia, an ally of the US, also sent troops to fight in South Vietnam.
draft.remember: Fear of communism spreading led the US from advisers to combat troops, with Australia joining in.

a.q: Why did the United States first become involved in Vietnam?
opts: It feared communism would spread to neighbouring countries
It wanted to take over the former French colony
It had been asked to by the French government after 1954
It was attacked by North Vietnamese forces in 1964
a.why: The domino theory held that one communist country would lead to others falling. The Gulf of Tonkin incident came in 1964, after US involvement had already begun with money, weapons and advisers, so it was not the first reason.

b.q: Which change did the Gulf of Tonkin incident of 1964 lead to?
opts: Congress let Johnson use force, and combat troops followed
The US began sending advisers to train South Vietnam's army
The US formally declared war on North Vietnam
Australia became the first country to send combat troops
b.why: The resolution gave Johnson power to use military force, and the first combat troops landed in 1965. Advisers were already in South Vietnam before 1964, so that option describes the earlier stage. No war was declared, because the resolution let Johnson act without one.

a.best: It feared communism would spread to neighbouring countries

b.best: Congress let Johnson use force, and combat troops followed

problems.detail: 'At first the US gave money and weapons and sent military advisers to train South Vietnam's army' suggests US involvement began with South Vietnam. In fact it began around 1950, when the US funded the French war in Indochina and set up an advisory group (MAAG). Year 12 HSC students may meet this in sources. Consider adding 'after 1954' or noting the earlier aid to France.

proposal.title: United States involvement
card: The United States feared that if one country in Southeast Asia became communist, its neighbours would follow, like falling dominoes. This idea, called the domino theory, was the main reason for US involvement in Vietnam.

From about 1950 the US paid for much of France's war against the Viet Minh. After 1954 it gave money, weapons and military advisers to South Vietnam. The advisers trained its army and were not sent as combat troops.

In August 1964, US ships reported attacks by North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin. Congress then passed a resolution that let President Johnson use military force in Vietnam without a declaration of war.
In 1965 the first US combat troops landed. Australia, an ally of the US, also sent troops to fight in South Vietnam.
proposal.remember: Fear of communism spreading took the US from aid and advisers to combat troops, with Australia joining in.

a.q: Why did the United States first become involved in Vietnam?
opts: It feared communism would spread to neighbouring countries
It wanted to gain a new colony in Southeast Asia
It needed Vietnam's rubber and rice for its own economy
It was attacked by North Vietnamese forces in 1964
a.why: The domino theory held that one communist country would lead its neighbours to fall too, and this fear drove US aid from about 1950. The Gulf of Tonkin incident came in 1964, long after US involvement had begun, so it cannot be the first reason.

Australia became the first country to send combat troops
b.why: The resolution gave Johnson power to use military force, and the first combat troops landed in 1965. Advisers were already in South Vietnam before 1964, so that option describes an earlier stage. No war was declared, because the resolution let Johnson act without one.
